conversation.content: Design a real-time chat system like Slack. Users send messages in channels and DMs, with real-time delivery. I expect you to drive this conversation.
Sure. Let me clarify a few things. How many users, concurrent connections, and messages per second? What's the max channel size? Do we need threading, reactions, file sharing, or just plain messages?
50M DAU, 5M concurrent connections, 100K messages per second. Max channel size 5000 members. Text messages and file sharing — skip threading and reactions.

The core challenge is real-time delivery. I'd use WebSockets for persistent bidirectional connections. When a user opens the app, they establish a WebSocket to our gateway. Messages flow through the WebSocket in both directions. The architecture: WebSocket gateways (stateful, hold connections), a Message Service (orchestration), a database for persistence, and a notification service for offline users.
5M concurrent WebSocket connections. How many gateway servers, and how does a message from User A reach User B who's on a different gateway?

At 100K connections per gateway, we'd need about 50 gateways. For routing: we need a lookup — which gateway is User B connected to? A connection registry in Redis: user_id → gateway_id. When User A sends a message to User B, the Message Service looks up User B's gateway in Redis and forwards the message there. The gateway pushes it down User B's WebSocket.
What about channels with 5000 members? User A posts in a channel — the message needs to reach 5000 people, potentially on 50 different gateways.

For channels, we can't look up 5000 user-to-gateway mappings individually — that's too many Redis queries. Better approach: use a pub/sub system. Each channel has a pub/sub topic (Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka). Each gateway subscribes to the channels of its connected users. When a message is posted to a channel, it's published to the topic, and all subscribed gateways receive it and deliver to their local connected members. But... with 5000 members across 50 gateways, that's basically every gateway subscribing to every popular channel. The pub/sub fanout might not save much.
Good observation. At staff level, how would you actually solve this efficiently?

Hmm, I think Redis Pub/Sub is still the right approach — the message is published once and Redis handles the multicast to subscribed gateways. The number of actual network messages is 50 (one per gateway) not 5000 (one per member). Each gateway then does local fan-out to its connected channel members. So the cost is O(gateways) not O(members). For very popular channels, that's a big saving. The gateway maintains a local mapping of channel_id → [connected user WebSockets] and delivers locally.
Good analysis. Where do you store messages persistently?

Cassandra. Partition key is channel_id (or conversation_id for DMs), clustering key is message_timestamp or a sequence number. This gives us ordered reads per channel — 'show me the last 50 messages in #engineering' — with high write throughput. Cassandra handles our 100K writes/sec easily across a small cluster.
You used timestamp as the clustering key. Two messages arrive at the same millisecond in the same channel. What happens?

They'd collide or be arbitrarily ordered. I should use a sequence number instead — a monotonically increasing counter per channel. But maintaining a distributed counter per channel across multiple Message Service instances is tricky. A centralized sequence generator would work but might be a bottleneck...
How would you solve the distributed counter problem?

Redis INCR on a key per channel? It's fast and atomic. But it's another Redis dependency and adds latency to every message. Alternatively, use a Snowflake-like ID — timestamp + machine ID + sequence counter — which is locally generated and globally unique. It doesn't guarantee strict ordering across servers, but within a single server it's ordered. Combined with the timestamp component, it provides a close-enough ordering. For most chat use cases, 'close enough' ordering is acceptable — users won't notice a 1ms reorder.
At staff level, 'close enough' isn't a satisfying answer for message ordering. But let's move on. How do you handle offline message delivery?

When a user reconnects, they need to catch up on missed messages. The client sends its last known message ID for each channel. The server queries Cassandra for messages newer than that ID and sends them. For push notifications while offline, we integrate with APNs and FCM. When a message arrives for an offline user, the notification service sends a push. We batch notifications to avoid spamming — 'You have 15 new messages in 3 channels' rather than 15 separate pushes.
What if a gateway server crashes?

100K users disconnect. They reconnect to other gateways automatically — the load balancer routes them. The connection registry entries for the dead gateway expire via TTL. New registrations overwrite stale ones. Messages sent during the disconnection window are in Cassandra — the users catch up via the sync protocol on reconnect. No message loss.
We're out of time. Anything to add?

File sharing — upload to S3, store the URL in the message. Search — index messages in Elasticsearch for full-text search across channels. And presence — show who's online, using a heartbeat-based system with Redis TTLs.
Thanks. Solid on the core messaging architecture, but the message ordering and sequence generation needed more depth for staff level.

strengths: Good channel fan-out analysis — correctly identified O(gateways) vs O(members) optimization with pub/sub + local delivery
Clean Cassandra schema design with appropriate partition and clustering keys
Practical gateway failure recovery with TTL-based registry cleanup
weaknesses: Message ordering was the weakest area — settled for 'close enough' with Snowflake IDs instead of designing a proper solution
Didn't discuss E2E encryption — a major feature for any modern chat system
No discussion of read receipts, typing indicators, or presence system beyond bullet points
Capacity estimation was minimal — mentioned 50 gateways but didn't size storage, bandwidth, or database cluster
Didn't drive the conversation proactively as expected at staff level
